Dear President Frederiksen,

I write to express my concerns regarding the University of New Haven (UNH) Tagliatela College of Engineering’s partnership with Xi’an University of Posts and Telecommunications (XUPT) in the People’s Republic of China (PRC) through the UNH-XUPT School of Information Engineering. Considering the facts outlined below, I urge UNH to terminate its joint cooperative program with XUPT.1

The UNH-XUPT School of Information Engineering was established in May 2025 with the approval of the Chinese Ministry of Education and is co-located on XUPT’s campus in Xi’an, China.2 The joint school is housed within XUPT’s College of Communications and Information Engineering. The joint school offers three undergraduate majors in strategically significant technology fields: communications engineering, data science and big data technology, and intelligence science and technology. Approximately one-third of the courses within each major are drawn from UNH’s curriculum and taught by UNH faculty.3 By operating in China, the UNH- XUPT joint school exists under PRC law and jurisdiction and within China’s regulatory and political environment. Like other joint education institutions of this nature, it is subject to PRC oversight and governance requirements and operates within a system that requires foreign educational partnerships to conform to China’s national education policies and broader strategic priorities.4 Accordingly, despite UNH’s participation, the joint school operates on Chinese soil,

XUPT’s own announcement places the partnership within the context of the PRC’s broader national development objectives. The university describes the joint school against the backdrop of the “deep implementation” of China’s “Belt and Road Initiative” and states that XUPT has aligned itself with national strategies and local economic and social development needs by leveraging its disciplinary strengths in the information and communications technology field.5 Accordingly, UNH is not merely participating in a traditional student-exchange arrangement. It is providing American university curriculum and faculty instruction in advanced technology disciplines through a jointly operated school located on the campus of a PRC university that publicly describes its activities as serving Chinese national strategies and development priorities.6,7

XUPT’s College of Communications and Information Engineering, where the UNH-XUPT joint school resides, openly promotes its support for China’s “military-civil fusion” (军民融合) strategy, with related innovations showcased at national conferences.8,9 The College also promotes its relationship with the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) National University of Defense Technology (NUDT) and the BeiDou Open Laboratory Xi’an Branch. At one jointly organized event, BeiDou Open Laboratory provided XUPT with RMB 300,000 worth of satellite-navigation simulation software and open-source receiver code to support research by XUPT faculty and students. XUPT’s own description makes the purpose of these activities clear: the College seeks to “vigorously promote the military-civilian integration development strategy” through BeiDou research while building a platform for talent cultivation, application development, technology transfer, and incubation.10 XUPT thus describes an institutional framework that connects its faculty, students, and laboratories with PLA expertise, technology, and industry in furtherance of China’s military-civil fusion strategy.11

XUPT’s College of Communications and Information Engineering maintains a longstanding institutional partnership with ZTE Corporation that integrates university and company research, laboratories, technical resources, faculty development, and student training. Beginning in 2015, XUPT and ZTE jointly established an ICT Innovation Practice Center on XUPT’s campus that supported internships, practical training, and graduation projects for communications engineering students. The relationship expanded through a 2020 cooperation agreement, and, in 2021, the parties agreed to further integrate their laboratory and educational resources in 5G, artificial intelligence, IoT, cloud computing, and big data. Among other activities, XUPT and ZTE agreed to jointly develop laboratories and courses, share 5G-related laboratory resources, conduct regular joint teaching and research activities, provide technical training to XUPT faculty, and establish what XUPT described as a “stable, win-win long-term mechanism” for university-enterprise cooperation.12 • ZTE has previously been subject to significant U.S. export control and sanctions enforcement. In 2017, ZTE agreed to a combined $1.19 billion settlement with the Departments of Justice, Commerce, and Treasury after admitting to illegally shipping U.S.origin goods to Iran in violation of U.S. sanctions and export control laws. XUPT’s own internal documents demonstrate that its connections to China’s defense research apparatus extend to the institutional level. XUPT maintains procedures governing the use of its Level II Confidentiality Qualification for Weapons and Equipment Scientific Research and Production Units and Weapons and Equipment Quality Management System Certificate, specialized credentials associated with participation in China’s weapons and equipment research and production system.19 XUPT also maintains an institutional framework for conducting

These are not standard research credentials held by all Chinese universities. Rather, they are specialized qualifications associated with institutions participating in China’s weapons and equipment research and production system. XUPT’s maintenance of a Level II Confidentiality Qualification for Weapons and Equipment Scientific Research and Production Units, together with a Weapons and Equipment Quality Management System Certificate, demonstrates an institutional capability to support defense-related research subject to specialized confidentiality and quality-management requirements.22 XUPT’s own procedures further require its Confidentiality Office to control the use of these credentials, underscoring that these qualifications are distinct from ordinary university research administration.23

The UNH-XUPT joint school is particularly concerning given UNH’s role in supporting U.S. cybersecurity education and workforce development. UNH has been designated a National Security Agency (NSA) Center of Academic Excellence in Cyber Operations since 2019, and its Tagliatela College of Engineering received an NSA National Centers of Academic Excellence in Cybersecurity grant to lead a coalition of five U.S. colleges and universities in preparing individuals for careers in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and cyber threat analysis.2425 Against the backdrop of XUPT’s College of Communications and Information Engineering’s documented relationships with the PLA, China’s defense research and industrial base, and military-civil fusion initiatives, the joint school creates a potential pathway for U.S.supported human and intellectual capital, expertise, and technical knowledge to benefit PRC strategic and technological priorities. This risk is particularly significant because XUPT itself has publicly framed the UNH partnership in the context of advancing its strategic priorities and implementing China’s Belt and Road Initiative and supporting military-civil fusion strategy.26

The overlap in research areas further heightens these concerns. As detailed earlier in this letter, XUPT faculty conducts research in areas including malware and cyberattack detection, communications jamming and anti-jamming, eavesdropping and covert communications, network intrusion detection, GNSS spoofing, and secure communications, including research conducted with PRC military and defense entities. These research areas overlap with cybersecurity and cyber operations disciplines encompassed by UNH’s NSA designation and federally supported cybersecurity programs. The result is a joint academic program connecting an NSA-designated U.S. cybersecurity institution with a PRC university’s subordinate College of Communications and Information Engineering whose faculty conduct research in extremely sensitive technical fields alongside PLA and defense-affiliated entities. The specific institution UNH has chosen as its partner presents too great a risk for the exploitation and diversion of American human and intellectual capital. U.S. universities should not support, conduct research with, or use federal research dollars to sustain institutional partnerships with foreign universities that maintain extensive relationships with Chinese military and defense entities.

This concern is especially acute here. A U.S. university whose engineering college is an NSA-designated Center of Academic Excellence in Cyber Operations should not maintain a joint academic program with a Chinese institution whose College of Communications and Information Engineering, the very college where the UNH-XUPT joint program resides, has faculty conducting extensive research in areas such as malware, cyberattack and network-intrusion detection, communications jamming and anti-jamming, eavesdropping, covert communications, and GNSS spoofing, including research with PLA and defense-affiliated entities. Such a partnership creates an unnecessary risk that American taxpayer-supported human and intellectual capital could be diverted to China’s defense research ecosystem.
This partnership puts the national security interests of the United States at risk. I therefore urge you to shut down UNH’s joint program with XUPT expeditiously.
Sincerely,
